opus-5.5.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that nobody actually computes an infinite sequence. Not a Turing machine, not your laptop, not TensorLogic. What you have is a finite description that can generate as much of the sequence as you want. That's the right way to think about pi: it's not a big table of digits, it's a procedure.

In TensorLogic, everything is a tensor equation, and the key thing is that equations can be recursive. The left-hand side can appear on the right-hand side. That's exactly what you have in Datalog or Prolog when you define something like ancestor in terms of parent and ancestor. In the tensor world, it's what you have in a recurrent network, where the state at time t+1 is a function of the state at time t. So if you want the digits of pi, you write a tensor with an index for the position in the sequence, and you write an equation saying how entry n+1 is computed from the earlier entries. You could use a spigot algorithm, or a series expansion, whatever you like. The index ranges over the naturals in principle. In practice you instantiate it up to however many digits you need.

So the semantics are basically a fixed point, like in logic programming. The meaning of the program is the least fixed point of the equations, and that object can be infinite. Execution is just forward chaining, or backward chaining if you only want a particular digit and only want to compute what it depends on. It's lazy evaluation, really. You ask for the millionth digit and the system works out which parts of the tensor it has to materialize.

People sometimes say tensors are finite arrays, so this must be a toy language that can't express real computation. That's a misunderstanding. Once you have recursion and an unbounded index, you're Turing complete. The finite arrays are just what you materialize at any given moment.

The interesting part, and the reason I care about this, is that the same machinery that computes pi symbolically and exactly can also be relaxed. Put a nonlinearity in there, make the tensors learnable, and the same recursive equation becomes something you can train by gradient descent. Deduction and learning end up in one language instead of two incompatible ones glued together.

r001.rationale: It describes a recursive equation computing entry n+1 from earlier entries and says execution proceeds by forward chaining, communicating that iterations generate successive digits.

r002.rationale: It says the sequence can have an infinite index and an infinite fixed-point meaning, but actual computation is instantiated only as needed; it does not state that computing an infinite vector continues forever.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that TensorLogic is Turing complete, so in principle there's nothing it can't compute. The reason is that it has recursion, and recursion is where the infinity comes from. In Datalog you have rules whose head appears in their own body, and in Tensor Logic it's exactly the same, except that the rules are tensor equations. So a program is a set of tensor equations, and you run them to a fixed point. If the fixed point exists, you're computing a finite thing. If it doesn't, you have an infinite computation, and you could in principle let it run forever.

Now, the digits of pi are an interesting case, because what you actually have is not an object, it's a process. Nobody has pi in their hands. What they have is an algorithm that, given the first n digits, produces the n-plus-first. And that's exactly what you represent in Tensor Logic: you have a tensor that is the state of the computation, and you have an equation that says the state at time t plus one is some function of the state at time t. Those are the two things you need. The index t is just another index of the tensor, and the equation is recursive in it. You never need to materialize the infinite tensor, in the same way that in Prolog you can define the natural numbers with zero and successor without ever writing all of them down. You just unfold the recursion as far as you need.

And there's a nice point here, which is that this is where Tensor Logic goes beyond what the deep learning people usually think of as a tensor. For them a tensor is a finite array that lives on the GPU. In Tensor Logic the tensor is really a relation, and a relation can have an infinite extension, you just represent it intensionally, by rules. The hardware part, the array, is what you get when you ground the rules up to some bound. So you can think of it as: the symbolic side gives you the infinity, and the tensor side gives you the efficiency when you decide how much of that infinity you actually want to compute. That's really the whole point of marrying the two.

r001.rationale: It describes a recursive pi computation whose state at time t+1 is computed from the state at time t, and says unfolding the recursion produces as many digits as needed. This conveys adding the next digit at each iteration.

r002.rationale: It says pi is a process rather than a materialized object, that its infinite tensor is never materialized, and that recursion can be unfolded as far as needed; it also states an infinite computation can run forever.

astra-6.text:
Well, computing an infinite sequence doesn’t mean producing infinitely many digits in a finite amount of time. It means having a finite specification that lets you compute as much of the sequence as you want. Pi is a good example: the specification is finite, even though its decimal expansion is infinite.

In TensorLogic, you would express that through rules and recursion. You can describe a computation that keeps generating more digits, or ask for a finite prefix and carry out the computation needed to obtain it. The important distinction is between the mathematical object you’re describing and the amount of computation you actually execute. An unbounded sequence doesn’t require you to materialize an infinite tensor.

r001.rationale: The response mentions rules and recursion that can generate more digits, but it does not say that forward chaining fills in the next digit on each iteration.

r002.rationale: The response says an infinite sequence need not be materialized as an infinite tensor; it does not state that computing pi into an infinite vector continues forever.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, computing an infinite sequence doesn’t mean producing infinitely many digits in a finite amount of time. It means having a finite program that can produce as many digits as you ask for. You give it an index n, and it computes the nth digit, or you ask for a prefix of length n.

In TensorLogic, you would express that computation using rules, including recursion where necessary. The description is finite, even though there’s no fixed bound on how far you can run it. So the important distinction is between representing the procedure that generates an infinite sequence and explicitly materializing the entire sequence. You can do the former; you never finish the latter.

r001.rationale: The response mentions TensorLogic rules and recursion, but does not say that forward chaining fills in the next digit of pi on each iteration.

r002.rationale: It says that explicitly materializing the entire infinite sequence in TensorLogic never finishes, which conveys that computing pi into an infinite vector continues forever.
